summary:
Solis turns NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS active-fire observations into a consistent record of burning activity across Brazil, since 2000. VIIRS, with 375 m pixels, detects smaller fires than MODIS (1 km). Their observations are not directly comparable, and switching sensors in 2012 creates an artificial increase of about 145% in the raw record.

Solis aggregates detections into daily 0.1° grid cells, counting each cell once per day. Using the 2012–2021 overlap period, a biome-calibrated machine-learning approach estimates what MODIS would have detected from VIIRS observations. Tested on years excluded from training, the harmonized record matches MODIS within 3.7% monthly across Brazil. The method was also tested in Australia, with 2.6% monthly error. Newer VIIRS observations, including NOAA-21, are linked through NOAA-20 with little added error. VIIRS-only detections remain in a separate layer, preserving information about smaller fires.

In the web app, users select a biome or define an area to explore burning calendars, seasonal patterns, unusual months, and long-term trends. A georeferenced map displays historical activity and near-real-time detections from NASA FIRMS and NOAA GOES-19. An experimental 7-day outlook is also available.

As MODIS approaches the end of its mission, Solis carries the fire record forward using VIIRS in comparable units, helping scientists, land managers, and emergency responders compare current activity with historical patterns.
details:
What it does

Solis is a web application that transforms NASA's MODIS and VIIRS active-fire observations into a consistent historical record of burning activity across Brazil, covering the period from 2000 to the present.

Users can select a Brazilian biome or define a custom area of interest to explore fire activity through an interactive calendar, historical comparisons, anomaly detection, seasonal patterns, and long-term trends with confidence intervals. The application also features a georeferenced map displaying historical fire activity and near-real-time detections, as well as an experimental seven-day fire outlook.

To complement its historical analysis, Solis integrates near-real-time observations from NOAA's GOES-19 satellite, with data updates every 10 minutes, and NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS).

How it works

Solis addresses a key challenge in long-term fire monitoring: MODIS and VIIRS observations cannot be directly compared because the sensors have different spatial resolutions and detection capabilities. MODIS has a spatial resolution of approximately 1 km, while VIIRS uses 375 m pixels and can detect smaller fires. Consequently, switching between these sensors can introduce artificial changes into a historical record. In Brazil, the raw record shows an increase of approximately 145% around the 2012 sensor transition, which does not represent an equivalent increase in actual fire activity.

To address this issue, Solis aggregates hotspot observations into daily records on a 0.1° grid. Each grid cell is counted only once per day, producing what the team calls a fire cell-day. When combining sensor observations, Solis uses a logical OR operation rather than adding detections together. This prevents multiple observations of the same grid cell on the same day from artificially inflating the activity count.

The harmonization approach uses machine learning to estimate what MODIS would have detected based on VIIRS observations. The model considers features such as VIIRS pixel count, fire radiative power (FRP), day or night observations, and neighboring grid cells.

The team evaluated three approaches: a ratio-based baseline, LightGBM, and a U-Net model. The validation strategy uses time-based data splits and held-out years to evaluate performance on periods excluded from training. The methodology also incorporates cross-fitting by year blocks, biome-specific calibration, and a correction for MODIS detections outside VIIRS coverage.

In monthly comparisons across Brazil, the harmonized record matches MODIS within 3.7% and removes the artificial discontinuity observed in the raw historical series. The method was also tested in Australia, achieving a 2.6% monthly error. Due to orbital drift affecting Terra and Aqua observations from 2022 onward, MODIS is used as the reference only through 2021.

Importantly, VIIRS-only detections are preserved in a separate layer rather than discarded during harmonization. This allows users to explore additional information about smaller fires that MODIS may not have detected. The approach also supports satellite continuity by linking NOAA-21 observations through NOAA-20, with very little additional error reported by the team.

Benefits and intended impact

As MODIS approaches the end of its operational life, maintaining continuity in long-term fire observations becomes increasingly important. Without a reliable way to harmonize observations from different sensors, historical records may become discontinuous or show misleading changes caused by differences in satellite capabilities rather than actual changes in fire activity.

Solis provides a bridge between MODIS and VIIRS, helping preserve a more consistent record of burning activity over time. Its interactive tools allow users to identify historical patterns, compare current activity with previous years, detect unusual conditions, and understand seasonal fire behavior.

The intended beneficiaries include scientists, environmental researchers, land managers, emergency responders, and other professionals who need accessible and comparable fire-activity information to support research, monitoring, planning, and decision-making.

What makes Solis creative

Solis goes beyond simply combining or rescaling satellite measurements. Its approach uses machine learning to estimate comparable MODIS-equivalent observations from VIIRS data while preserving VIIRS-only detections in a separate layer. This makes it possible to maintain historical comparability without losing information about smaller fires detected by the newer sensor.

The team also evaluated different modeling approaches, used time-separated validation to assess performance on unseen years, and calibrated the method for individual biomes. Testing the approach in Australia further explores its potential beyond the Brazilian dataset.

By bringing together a harmonized historical record, interactive data exploration, near-real-time satellite observations, and an experimental outlook, Solis offers multiple perspectives on fire activity through a single platform.

Tools and technologies

The backend and data-processing pipeline were developed in Python, using FastAPI for the API, DuckDB for data management, LightGBM and PyTorch for machine-learning development and evaluation, ONNX Runtime for model inference, and NumPy, pandas, and xarray for data processing.

The frontend was developed with TypeScript, React 19, Vite, and Tailwind CSS. Frontend API types are generated from a shared OpenAPI contract. The mapping interface uses geospatial data, Natural Earth geographic boundaries, and OpenStreetMap resources.

The project uses NASA MODIS and VIIRS active-fire products accessed through FIRMS, along with NOAA GOES-19 ABI fire and hot-spot observations. Model training used a laptop GPU and Google Colab, while the API runs on a CPU-only server. Discloud is used for API hosting.

AI-assisted development tools were also part of the team's workflow. Claude Code (Anthropic) assisted with backend development, data-pipeline helpers, model-training code, frontend integration, tests, and documentation. Figma Make was used to generate the initial frontend interface, which the team subsequently revised and connected to the API.

The team reviewed and tested the AI-assisted code. AI tools were not used to generate scientific datasets or numerical results; these come from the satellite and environmental data sources used by the project.

Factors considered

Throughout development, the team considered several limitations and sources of uncertainty. A satellite hotspot is not equivalent to a fire count or burned area. Cloud cover, satellite outages, and missing observations can affect the available data and should not be interpreted as evidence that no fire occurred.

The team also considered differences in sensor sensitivity, spatial resolution, observation schedules, and satellite orbital drift, as well as the additional detections provided by NOAA-20 and NOAA-21. Estimates for smaller areas may be less reliable than those calculated for larger biomes, which is an important consideration when interpreting results.

These factors informed the harmonization methodology, validation strategy, and presentation of the results. The team aimed to make the platform useful while communicating the limitations of satellite-based fire monitoring.
